newsitem.title: USA: U.S. utilities ready transmission data for cyberspace.
newsitem.headline: U.S. utilities ready transmission data for cyberspace.

text.p: The next competitive frontier in the U.S. power industry has shifted to cyberspace, where utilities are building Internet sites to post their prices for moving electricity across the nation's transmission grid.
"Everyone supports Internet access," said Gerry Cauley, manager of grid operations and planning at Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) at Palo Alto, Calif.
Under a plan by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), utilities must open their transmission grids to foster wholesale competition and, ultimately, cheaper power prices.

Utilities owning high-voltage transmission lines must also provide information sites called OASIS, where marketers and other new players in the deregulated market can find out how much transmission capacity is available on these lines.
"They're all based on Internet and Internet-based tools," said Cauley, referring to the OASIS systems.
EPRI, an industry group, aids electric technology research ranging from data system development to renewable generation.

Under FERC's plan, power providers would compete only in the cost of generating electricity since they all would pay the same price for transmission and have equal access to data via OASIS on line capacity needed to carry the load.
OASIS would also carry information on ancillary services like voltage control and frequency regulation.
FERC set a Dec. 2 deadline for testing of OASIS.
Twenty-five OASIS systems, or nodes, are expected to be operating on Jan 3, 1997, Cauley said. "Most of the nodes are in the late stages of development."

"Everybody in our membership is proceeding along fairly quickly," said Michael Gildea, senior regulatory analyst at the Edison Electric Institute, a trade group that represents investor-owned utilities (IOUs), which control most of nation's transmission grid and about 75 percent of power output.
OASIS was developed over the past two years by IOUs, publicly-owned utilities and marketers.

To use it, requests for transmission capacity are placed on an OASIS node. The regional transmission control operator, who oversees traffic on the grid, evaluates the request and replies on-line whether it is feasible, Gildea noted.
"We're almost there, but not yet," said Kandice Olsen, spokeswoman for Mid-American Interconnect Network which oversees transmission reliability in parts of upper Midwest.
Much of the transmission data would be available on the Internet, but security codes would be needed to access the information, Olsen said when asked about Mid-American's OASIS model.
A Mid-American committee has been working with software vendors and neighbouring power pools to develop standards for its real-time information system, she said.
Mid-American hoped to to input actual transmission rates on line by the end of year, Olsen said, adding its transmission-owning utilities were expected to pay for expenses related to OASIS.
While most utilities have jointly developed OASIS nodes, a few decided to operate their systems for security reasons.

"It's a matter of security we oppose sharing with other utilities," said Cory Warren, spokesman for Pacific Gas & Electric Co. in San Francisco. The utility had a headstart on developing OASIS because it has been running a similar electronic bulletin board since last year, he added.

The initial cost of a OASIS node was estimated at $300,000 to $500,000, according to industry sources. FERC has allowed utilities to recoup startup and running costs through the rates they charge for transmission on their lines.
